result: The study analyzed 1472 population-based data sources with measured height from over 18.6 million adults born 1896-1996 across 200 countries, covering 97% of the world's population. The study excluded self-reported height data to avoid systematic bias.
evaluation: Claims C3-C4 and C94-C122 collectively describe the study's comprehensive data collection methodology. The large sample size (18.6 million participants), broad geographic coverage (179 countries with data, 97% of world population), and use of only measured (not self-reported) height data provide a strong foundation for the analysis. The methodological rigor is well-documented.

result: The study employed a hierarchical Bayesian statistical model that characterized non-linear trends, weighted national data more heavily than subnational/community data, and performed extremely well in validation tests with unbiased estimates and 97% credible interval coverage.
evaluation: Claims C96-C130 describe the statistical methodology and validation. The hierarchical structure appropriately accounts for data quality differences, and the validation results (median errors near zero, 95% CI coverage of 97%) demonstrate excellent model performance. The methodological approach is sound and well-validated.

result: South Korean women had the largest height gain over the century (20.2 cm, 95% CI 17.5-22.7), moving from fifth shortest to top tertile globally. Iranian men had the largest male gain (16.5 cm, 95% CI 13.3-19.7), while South Korean men gained 15.2 cm (12.3-18.1).
evaluation: Claims C5-C6 and C35-C36 present the study's most dramatic findings with credible intervals. The magnitude of gains in South Korea and Iran represents the largest documented height increases globally over this period. These findings are supported by the comprehensive dataset and are consistent with known improvements in nutrition and living conditions in these countries.

result: Adult height showed little change or decreased in some sub-Saharan African countries and South Asia. In sub-Saharan Africa, height decreased by ~5 cm from peak levels for cohorts born after the early 1960s. South Asian countries plateaued 5-10 cm shorter than East Asian countries.
evaluation: Claims C7-C8 and C48-C49, C56-C57 document stagnation and decline in height in specific regions. The findings are supported by Figure 8 and are consistent with documented increases in childhood stunting in sub-Saharan Africa (C90). The contrast with East Asian gains highlights substantial global health inequalities.

result: In 1896, the shortest populations were in Asia and Central/Andean Latin America (men in Laos: 152.9 cm; women in Guatemala: 140.3 cm, equivalent to well-nourished 12.5-year and 10-year children respectively). The tallest were in Central/Northern Europe, North America, and Pacific islands (Swedish women: 160.3 cm; men in Sweden/Norway/USA: >171 cm).
evaluation: Claims C9-C10 and C25-C34, C131 establish baseline height distributions in 1896. The comparison to modern child growth standards (C26, C28) effectively illustrates the severity of historical malnutrition. The geographic patterns are well-documented and supported by Figures 1-2. The findings provide essential context for understanding century-long trends.

result: By 1996, Dutch men were the tallest globally (182.5 cm, 95% CI 180.6-184.5), while the shortest were men in Timor-Leste/Yemen/Laos (~160 cm) and women in Guatemala (149.4 cm, 95% CI 148.0-150.8). The global height gap was 22-23 cm for men (increased ~4 cm from 1896) and 20 cm for women (unchanged).
evaluation: Claims C61-C70 document 1996 height distributions with credible intervals. The persistence of a 20 cm gap for women and increase for men (C64-C65) demonstrates lack of global convergence despite substantial changes in country rankings. The findings are supported by comprehensive data and Figure 5.

result: The height differential between tallest and shortest populations was 19-20 cm a century ago and remained the same for women while increasing for men, with no indication of global convergence despite substantial changes in country rankings.
evaluation: Claims C11-C13 and C82-C85 establish a key finding: persistent global inequality in height. The lack of convergence despite dramatic changes in individual countries (e.g., South Korea's rise) indicates that improvements in some regions were offset by stagnation or decline in others. This is a well-supported major conclusion.

result: Large height gains occurred in Japan, Greenland, and Southern/Central Europe. However, Japan's rise stopped after the early 1960s, and South Korea's flattened in the 1980s for men and may be beginning for women. South Koreans now exceed Japanese in height, while Chinese have surpassed Japanese but not South Koreans.
evaluation: Claims C37-C47 document complex temporal patterns in East Asia with supporting Figure 6. The plateauing in Japan and South Korea is well-documented, though C43 appropriately uses tentative language ('may have') for the uncertain trend in South Korean women. The relative rankings are clearly established by the data.

result: Height plateaued in Northern Europe (Finland) and English-speaking countries (UK) for 2-3 decades, with the USA showing the smallest gain among high-income countries and falling behind European counterparts. In contrast, height continues increasing in Southern Europe (Spain) and Latin America.
evaluation: Claims C50-C55 document divergent trends in high-income Western countries, supported by Figure 7 and citations. The USA's poor performance relative to other high-income countries is particularly notable and consistent with prior research (C52-C53 cite supporting studies). The contrast with continuing gains in Southern Europe and Latin America is well-established.

result: Adult height decreased for men but not women in some Central Asian (Azerbaijan, Uzbekistan) and Middle East/North African countries (Egypt, Yemen), while both sexes continue growing taller in Iran.
evaluation: Claims C58-C60 document sex-specific trends in Central Asia and MENA. The sex difference in trends is notable and suggests gender-specific factors affecting nutrition or health. However, the claims appropriately use tentative language ('seems to have happened'), acknowledging some uncertainty. The contrast with Iran's continued gains is well-documented.

result: Male and female heights were correlated across countries in both 1896 and 1996. Men were consistently taller than women by ~11 cm (1896) and ~12 cm (1996). In 1896, the sex gap was larger in shorter populations, suggesting men had relative advantage in undernourished populations, but by 1996 the gap was uniform across height ranges. Changes in male and female heights were correlated over time.
evaluation: Claims C71-C77 document sex differences and their evolution, supported by Figure 9. The interpretation that men had relative advantage in undernourished populations (C75) is reasonable given the data pattern in C74, though it remains somewhat speculative. The correlation of height changes between sexes (C77) contrasts with BMI patterns, providing important insights into sex-specific responses to environmental changes.

result: Change in population mean height was not correlated with change in BMI for men (r=-0.016) and weakly inversely correlated for women (r=-0.28). Countries like Japan, Singapore, and France had large height gains with little BMI change, while USA and Kiribati had small height gains with large BMI increases.
evaluation: Claims C78-C81 document the independence of height and BMI trends, supported by Figure 10 and BMI data from another study. The lack of correlation indicates that factors driving height gains differ from those driving BMI increases. The specific country examples (C80-C81) effectively illustrate this dissociation. This is an important finding for understanding nutrition transitions.

result: Continental European countries have overtaken English-speaking countries like the USA in height, consistent with earlier studies, though this study provides more comprehensive coverage of Eastern and Southern Europe using only measured (not self-reported) data.
evaluation: Claims C86-C87 contextualize findings within prior research while noting methodological improvements. The consistency with earlier studies strengthens confidence in the results, while the expanded geographic coverage and use of measured data represent important advances. The comparison is appropriate and well-supported.

result: Height gains in South Korea and Japan may partially account for women in these countries achieving the first and fourth highest life expectancy globally.
evaluation: Claim C88 is speculative ('may partially account'), linking height gains to life expectancy outcomes. While C89 correctly states the life expectancy rankings and the association between height and mortality is established in the literature, the causal contribution of height gains to life expectancy in these specific countries is not directly tested. The claim appropriately uses tentative language but lacks direct supporting evidence.

result: Prior studies documented rising childhood stunting in sub-Saharan Africa through the mid-1990s, which may have carried forward to affect adult health. Africa's early height advantage over Asia may have been due to more diverse diet versus Asian cereal-based diet, but rising population and worsening economic conditions during structural adjustment may have undermined this advantage.
evaluation: Claims C90-C93 provide speculative interpretations of African height trends. While C90 correctly cites prior research on childhood stunting, C91-C93 use appropriately tentative language ('may have') for mechanistic explanations. The dietary and economic hypotheses are plausible and cite supporting literature, but remain speculative without direct evidence linking these factors to the observed height trends in this study.

result: Greater adult height is beneficially associated with cardiovascular/respiratory diseases but harmfully associated with certain cancers (colorectal, postmenopausal breast, ovarian, and possibly pancreatic/prostate/premenopausal breast), independent of BMI. If causal (supported by Mendelian randomization studies), the ~20 cm global height range associates with 17% lower cardiovascular mortality and 20-40% higher cancer risk in tall versus short countries.
evaluation: Claims C100-C106 summarize established associations from prior literature with extensive citations. The conditional nature of the risk estimates (C104-C105) is appropriate, and the support from Mendelian randomization studies (C106) strengthens causal inference. However, these are primarily literature review claims rather than new findings from this study. The quantitative estimates assume causality and extrapolate from individual-level to population-level effects.

result: Gains in mean population height in successive cohorts are associated with lower mortality in middle and older ages (r=-0.58 for men, r=-0.68 for women) in countries with reliable mortality data, demonstrating large impacts on population health and longevity.
evaluation: Claim C107 presents an original analysis linking height gains to mortality reduction, supported by Figure 11 and consistent with individual-level evidence. The correlation coefficients are substantial and the analysis is restricted to countries with reliable mortality data. This provides population-level evidence for the health benefits of height gains, though correlation does not prove causation.

result: Short maternal stature increases risk of small-for-gestational-age and preterm births (both risk factors for neonatal mortality) and pregnancy complications. Therefore, improvements versus stagnation in women's height can influence infant and maternal mortality trends.
evaluation: Claims C108-C110 cite established associations from prior research. Claim C111 is an inference connecting women's height trends to maternal/infant mortality outcomes. While the logic is sound and the underlying associations are well-established, this represents an interpretation rather than a direct finding from the current study. The inference is reasonable but not directly tested.

result: Adult height signifies foetal, childhood, and adolescent nutrition and links early-life experiences to NCDs, longevity, education, and earnings. Therefore, height in early adulthood provides a measurable indicator for sustainable development.
evaluation: Claims C112-C114 summarize established knowledge about height as a marker of early-life conditions and predictor of later outcomes, supported by citations. Claim C115 draws a reasonable conclusion that height can serve as a development indicator. While this is more of a conceptual/policy conclusion than an empirical finding, it is well-supported by the study's comprehensive documentation of height trends and their correlates.

result: Data in some countries were limited or from sub-national/community studies, reflected in larger uncertainty of height estimates in these countries.
evaluation: Claims C98-C99 acknowledge data limitations transparently. The hierarchical model appropriately accounts for data quality differences (C97, C123), and the validation results (C128-C130) demonstrate that the model handles sparse data well. The acknowledgment of uncertainty is appropriate and the study's approach to handling variable data quality is sound.

result: Being taller is associated with enhanced longevity, higher education and earnings, lower risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes and cardiovascular/respiratory diseases, and higher cancer risk. Height is highly heritable but cross-population differences relate to environmental factors, particularly foetal growth, childhood/adolescent nutrition, and infections.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C14-C24 provide background context from prior literature, all supported by citations. These establish the importance of studying height trends but are not original findings of this study. The claims accurately represent established knowledge and provide appropriate motivation for the research. C19 appropriately includes 'possibly' for the less certain association with social position.
